chapter.name: A Journey through States of Water

questions.q: Lata sprinkles a little water on a hot tawa before making dosa. A white cloud rises for a moment and the water is gone in seconds. Which statement explains the white cloud she sees?
questions.a: Water vapour formed, and tiny droplets in the steam make it visible
o: Water vapour formed, and tiny droplets in the steam make it visible
Water vapour is always white, so it can be seen wherever it forms
The water seeped into the iron tawa and came back out as smoke
The water froze into fine ice flakes in the hot air just above the tawa

questions.q: Kabir puts a tablespoon of water on a steel plate in his room on a cloudy day. He checks the underside every 30 minutes: it is dry each time, and after three hours the water on top has gone. Which conclusion do his observations support best?
questions.a: The water changed into water vapour and went into the air
o: The water changed into water vapour and went into the air
The water seeped through tiny holes in the steel plate and dried
Water can disappear like this only on a hot, sunny day
The water was destroyed, so it no longer exists anywhere

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A wet floor-mop left in a closed store-room, with no fan, no sunlight and no heater, is dry by the next morning.
Reason (R): Water left exposed changes into water vapour only when it is heated until it boils.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A bowl holding 500 mL of water is left in a closed store-room with no fan, no sunlight and no heater, and the shelf under it stays dry. After 3 days it holds 488 mL. On average, ___ mL of water changed into water vapour each day.
After a rainy morning, a puddle on the mud playground has become smaller by evening. Aavi says the soil absorbed it; Thirav says it evaporated. Which judgement is the most reasonable?
questions.a: Both can happen here: soil can soak up water, and water also evaporates
o: Both can happen here: soil can soak up water, and water also evaporates
Only soaking is possible, since evaporation needs the water to be boiled
Only evaporation is possible, since soil can never take in any water
Neither happens; the water slowly turns into invisible ice in the mud

questions.q:
In a class test, a tablespoon (15 mL) of water was placed on each of two surfaces kept side by side on a table: a steel plate and an unglazed clay tile. The students checked every 30 minutes.
Steel plate: underside dry at every check; top dry after 3 hours.
Clay tile: underside damp from the first check; top dry after 1 hour 30 minutes.
(a) Where did the water on the steel plate go?
(b) How many times as fast did the water vanish from the top of the tile as from the plate?
(c) Give the reason why the tile lost its water faster.
(d) A family wants to store water overnight and lose as little as possible. Which material does the data favour, and what can you say for the other choice?
questions.a: (a) It evaporated into the air as water vapour; nothing seeped through. (b) 3 hours divided by 1.5 hours = 2 times as fast. (c) On the tile, water seeped through the clay (the damp underside shows it) as well as evaporating, so it was lost by two routes. (d) Steel, since water was lost only by evaporation there. The clay loses more water, but it is not useless: water that seeps through an earthen pot and evaporates keeps the water inside cool, so a family may accept the loss for colder water.
s: (a) evaporated as water vapour, no seeping
(b) 3 / 1.5 = 2 times
(c) seeping through the clay plus evaporation
(d) Steel chosen for least loss, with a fair point for clay (cooler water)

questions.q: Arjun weighs a wet handkerchief at 250 g. He dries it on a hanger above a sheet of newspaper, which stays dry the whole time, and weighs it again when it is dry: 180 g. Which conclusion do his readings support?
questions.a: 70 g of water went into the air as water vapour
o: 70 g of water went into the air as water vapour
70 g of water was destroyed as the cloth dried
70 g of water soaked into the newspaper below it
70 g of the cotton cloth itself turned into vapour

questions.q: During a school day, four things happen. Which one is NOT an example of evaporation?
questions.a: An ice cube left in a cup on the table turning into water
o: An ice cube left in a cup on the table turning into water
Sweat on Ravi's forehead drying up after the PT period
A wet school uniform on the clothesline becoming dry
The mopped classroom floor becoming dry before lunch

questions.q:
Ritu weighs a wet towel at intervals as it hangs on the balcony. The same towel weighs 400 g when completely dry.
8 a.m.: 640 g; 10 a.m.: 520 g; 12 noon: 430 g; 2 p.m.: 400 g; 4 p.m.: 400 g.
(a) What percentage of the towel's water had left it by 10 a.m.?
(b) Her brother says the towel stopped drying after 2 p.m. because evaporation stops in the afternoon. Use the data to give the real reason.
(c) Ritu's bus leaves at 1 p.m. Her mother says the towel may be packed only if it holds no more than 20 g of water. Assuming it dries at a steady rate between noon and 2 p.m., can Ritu pack it at 12:30 p.m.? Find the earliest time it could be packed.
questions.a: (a) The towel held 640 - 400 = 240 g of water; 640 - 520 = 120 g had gone by 10 a.m., which is 50%. (b) At 2 p.m. the towel already weighed its dry mass of 400 g, so no water was left to evaporate; evaporation had not stopped. (c) No. Between noon and 2 p.m. it lost 30 g, or 15 g per hour. At 12:30 it has lost 7.5 g more and still holds 30 - 7.5 = 22.5 g of water, more than the 20 g limit. To get down to 20 g it must lose 10 g after noon, which takes 10 / 15 hour = 40 minutes, so the earliest time is 12:40 p.m., ten minutes after she must pack.
s: (b) the towel had reached its dry mass, so no water was left to evaporate
(c) 15 g per hour, so 22.5 g left at 12:30, above 20 g: she cannot pack it then; earliest 12:40 p.m.

questions.q:
Neel weighs his wet school shirt at 600 g and hangs it in a closed bathroom; the floor below stays dry. When the shirt is dry it weighs 350 g.
(a) How much water left the shirt, and in what form did it leave?
(b) Neel's sister says, 'That water has been destroyed.' Correct her.
questions.a: (a) 600 - 350 = 250 g of water left the shirt as water vapour. (b) The water is not destroyed. It has only changed its state into water vapour, which is now part of the water vapour in the air of the bathroom.
s: Part (a): 250 g, as water vapour
Part (b): not destroyed; it changed state and is now in the air as water vapour

questions.q:
Read the statements about water disappearing.
Statement 1: Water evaporates only when it is heated to boiling, as on a dosa pan.
Statement 2: The water vapour formed when clothes dry is normally invisible to us.
Statement 3: Hand sanitiser vanishing as it is rubbed on the hands is a liquid changing into vapour.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: True or False? A chart coloured with pencil colours must be left to dry before it is rolled up, just like a chart painted with watercolours. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Watercolours put water on the paper, and that water has to evaporate before the chart is dry. Pencil colours put no water on the paper, so there is nothing to evaporate and the chart can be rolled up at once.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: only the watercolour chart carries water that must evaporate; pencil colours leave no water

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the best explanation in Column II.
Column I
1. A watercolour painting can be stacked after an hour without smudging
2. Water on an unglazed clay tile makes its underside damp
3. A kulfi left on a plate becomes runny
4. A white haze rises above a pot of boiling dal
Column II
a. Water vapour made visible by tiny droplets of water
b. Water seeping through the surface
c. A solid changing into a liquid; no evaporation
d. The water in it has evaporated
Ravi says, 'The white cloud above the spout of a boiling kettle is water vapour. That proves water vapour can always be seen.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Steam is indeed water vapour, so he is right that the cloud comes from water changing into vapour. But water vapour itself is invisible; the cloud is visible only because some of the vapour in the steam has turned into tiny water droplets. The water vapour from a drying shirt or a mopped floor cannot be seen at all.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: steam is water vapour formed from the boiling water
Wrong part: vapour is invisible; tiny droplets in the steam make it visible, as drying clothes show

questions.q:
Ira rubs hand sanitiser on her palms. Within seconds it vanishes, and her palms are left dry.
(a) What change has the sanitiser undergone?
(b) Her brother says only water can evaporate. Use Ira's observation to test his idea.
questions.a: (a) The liquid sanitiser has changed into vapour: it has evaporated. (b) He is wrong. Sanitiser is not water, yet it vanished from her palms by changing into vapour, so liquids other than water also evaporate.
s: Part (a): the liquid sanitiser evaporated (changed into vapour)
Part (b): sanitiser is not water but it evaporated, so other liquids evaporate too

questions.q:
Water sprinkled on a hot dosa tawa is gone in about 3 seconds. The same amount spilled on the kitchen floor takes about 15 minutes to dry. Gopi says, 'Only the tawa shows evaporation; the floor is not hot, so that water must have gone some other way.'
(a) Is the change the same in both places? Give a reason.
(b) What does the floor show that the tawa cannot?
questions.a: (a) Yes. In both places liquid water changes into water vapour, which is evaporation; the hot tawa only makes it happen much faster. (b) The floor shows that evaporation takes place even at room temperature, with no heating at all.
s: Part (a): yes, both are water changing into vapour; heat only makes it faster
Part (b): evaporation goes on even at room temperature

questions.q:
Aavi wants to know whether water seeps through a plastic lunch-box lid. She rests the lid on a sheet of dry tissue paper, puts a tablespoon of water on it and checks every 20 minutes. After 2 hours the water on the lid has gone and the tissue is still dry.
(a) What two conclusions can she draw from this?
(b) Her friend repeats the test with the lid resting on a wet kitchen counter. Why would his result tell him nothing about seeping?
questions.a: (a) No water seeped through the plastic lid, since the tissue under it stayed dry; the water on top changed into water vapour and went into the air (it evaporated). (b) The counter is already wet, so the underside of the lid would be wet whether or not any water came through it. He could not tell seeped water apart from the water already on the counter.
s: Part (a): nothing seeped through (tissue dry), and the water evaporated into the air
Part (b): a wet surface below hides any seeped water, so the test cannot decide

questions.q: Write a situation from your home or school, not about a steel plate or a puddle, in which water disappears by evaporation without being heated. Then name one observation in your situation that would show the water did not seep away, and say where the water has gone.
questions.a: For example: washed steel glasses are left upside down on a plastic rack in the kitchen and are dry in an hour. The tray under the rack stays dry, so the water did not drip or seep away. The water has changed into water vapour and gone into the air of the kitchen, even though nothing was heated.
s: A realistic situation of water drying with no heating (not a plate or puddle)
An observation ruling out seepage, e.g. the surface or tray below stays dry
The water has gone into the air as water vapour

questions.q:
After rain at 8 a.m., the school measures two puddles of the same size, both in the open sun. One is on the cemented basketball court: cement does not let water soak in, and the ground under the puddle is dry when it has gone. The other is on the mud ground. The court puddle is gone by 3 p.m.; the mud puddle is gone by 12 noon. Aavi says puddles disappear because the soil absorbs the water; Thirav says they evaporate.
(a) What does the court puddle show on its own?
(b) The mud puddle went 3 hours sooner. What does this extra speed suggest, and why can it not be put down to the sun?
(c) Whose idea explains the puddles? Give a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: (a) Water can disappear by evaporation alone: nothing soaked into the cement, yet the puddle vanished in 7 hours. (b) On the mud the water was lost by a second route as well: some soaked into the soil while some evaporated. The sun cannot explain the difference, because both puddles were the same size and in the same open sun. (c) Neither idea alone is complete. Thirav's idea explains the court puddle, but the mud puddle needs both: soaking into the ground and evaporation together, which is why it went faster.
s: (a) evaporation alone can remove the court puddle, as nothing soaked in
(b) a second route, soaking into the soil, adds to evaporation on mud
(b) same size and same sun, so the sun is not the cause
(c) judgement that both processes act on mud
(c) evaporation alone explains the court, so neither idea is complete alone

questions.q: Over one Sunday, Rhea notes six activities at home: (i) drying papads on the terrace; (ii) making ice in the freezer; (iii) leaving washed steel plates on a rack; (iv) melting butter for halwa; (v) colouring a chart with watercolours; (vi) wiping the floor with a wet mop. Pick the activities that depend on evaporation, say why the other two do not, and explain for any one of your picks how you know evaporation is taking place.
questions.a: Evaporation: (i), (iii), (v) and (vi), since in each, water is left on a surface and disappears into the air as water vapour. Not evaporation: (ii) is liquid water changing into ice and (iv) is solid butter changing into liquid; neither turns a liquid into vapour. For example, in (vi) the wet floor becomes dry without any heating and the water is not seen going anywhere: it has changed into invisible water vapour.
s: Picks (i), (iii), (v) and (vi)
Rejects (ii) and (iv): liquid to solid and solid to liquid, not liquid to vapour
Explains one pick: water disappears into the air as invisible vapour

questions.q:
Classify each of these as evaporation or not evaporation, and give a reason for each.
(i) A wet saree on a clothesline becomes dry.
(ii) Butter in a hot pan turns runny.
(iii) Hand sanitiser vanishes as it is rubbed on the palms.
(iv) Water drops appear on the outside of a bottle taken out of the fridge.
(v) Water sprinkled on a hot tawa vanishes with a hiss.
questions.a: (i) Evaporation: the water in the saree changes into water vapour. (ii) Not evaporation: a solid is changing into a liquid. (iii) Evaporation: the liquid sanitiser changes into vapour. (iv) Not evaporation: water vapour from the air is changing into liquid drops on the cold bottle, the reverse change. (v) Evaporation: the water changes into steam (water vapour).
s: (i) evaporation, water to vapour
(ii) not evaporation: solid to liquid
(iii) evaporation, liquid sanitiser to vapour
(iv) not evaporation: vapour turning into liquid on a cold surface
(v) evaporation: water to steam

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When Rahul steps out of an air-conditioned car into a humid street in Kolkata, his spectacles are at once covered with tiny drops.
Reason (R): When water vapour present in the air comes in contact with a cold surface, it forms water droplets.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: At 6:30 a.m. the school lawn is covered with dew, though it did not rain. By 10 a.m. the grass is dry, and the next morning there is dew again. Which explanation fits the whole cycle?
questions.a: Overnight vapour in the air condenses on the cool grass; by day the drops evaporate
o: Overnight vapour in the air condenses on the cool grass; by day the drops evaporate
Overnight the drops evaporate onto the grass; by day they condense back into the air
The grass gives out water at night and soaks the same water back in during the day
Dew is a light rain that falls only at dawn and then seeps down into the soil

questions.q: A covered glass of iced water stands on a balance. Over 30 minutes the reading rises from 410.0 g to 411.8 g, drops gather on the outside, and the water level stays exactly at a line marked on the glass. Show that the drops cannot have come from water seeping out of the glass.
questions.a: If water had seeped out, the level inside would have fallen below the mark, but it did not. Seepage also cannot add mass, since it only moves water from inside to outside; yet the mass rose by 411.8 - 410.0 = 1.8 g. So the 1.8 g of water outside must have come from water vapour in the air condensing on the cold glass.
s: The level did not fall below the mark, so no water left the inside
The mass rose by 1.8 g, which seepage cannot cause
Conclusion: the drops are condensed water vapour from the air

questions.q: On a cold winter morning, Tsering finds drops of water on the leaves in the garden and on the windscreen of the parked car. It did not rain at night and nobody watered the garden. Which explanation fits both observations?
questions.a: Water vapour in the air condensed on the cold surfaces
o: Water vapour in the air condensed on the cold surfaces
Water from inside the leaves and the glass seeped out
The night air froze on them and then slowly melted
Water evaporated onto the leaves and glass overnight

questions.q: Pooja wants to check whether any water seeps out of a cold container. If 3 mL of water seeped out, the level in her wide tumbler would fall by only 0.2 cm, too little to notice, but in a tall, narrow bottle the same 3 mL would make the level fall by 1.8 cm. Using the bottle makes the same loss show up as a fall ___ times as large.

After Leena's hot bath, the bathroom mirror is covered with tiny drops, but the dry towel hanging beside it is not.
(a) Name, in order, the two changes of state the water goes through on its way from the hot bath water to the mirror.
(b) Why do the drops form on the mirror?
questions.a: (a) First evaporation: the hot water changes into water vapour. Then condensation: the vapour changes back into liquid droplets. (b) The mirror is a cold surface compared with the steamy air; water vapour forms droplets when it comes in contact with a cold surface.
s: Part (a): evaporation (water to vapour), then condensation (vapour to droplets)
Part (b): vapour touching the cold surface of the mirror forms droplets

questions.q: The bathroom mirror at Leena's house is covered with drops after she takes a hot-water bath, but stays clear after her brother takes a cold-water bath in the same bathroom. Which explanation fits both observations?
questions.a: Hot water evaporates fast, filling the air with vapour that condenses on the cool mirror
o: Hot water evaporates fast, filling the air with vapour that condenses on the cool mirror
Cold bath water makes the mirror colder, and vapour never condenses on a very cold surface
Hot water splashes up onto the mirror, while cold water is too heavy to splash so high
Steam from the hot bath seeps through the mirror glass from the wall behind it

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in the air.
Statement 2: Rainy days are usually less humid than dry, sunny days.
Statement 3: Dew drops seen on plants are formed by condensation of water vapour from the air.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Aavi covers a glass tumbler half-filled with water and ice cubes with a small steel plate and puts it on a digital balance. She records the reading every 5 minutes.
0 min 486.0 g; 5 min 486.4 g; 10 min 486.9 g; 15 min 487.3 g; 20 min 487.8 g; 25 min 488.2 g; 30 min 488.6 g.
(a) What was the average rise in the reading for each 5 minutes?
(b) If the trend continues, about what will the reading be at 35 minutes?
(c) Thirav says the data prove that no water seeped through the tumbler wall. Judge his claim, and name the one change to the set-up that would settle the question.
questions.a: (a) The total rise is 488.6 - 486.0 = 2.6 g over six 5-minute intervals, about 2.6 / 6 = 0.43 g each. (b) About 488.6 + 0.43 = 489.0 g. (c) He is not right. The rise shows that water came from the air, but seepage only moves water from inside the tumbler to its outer surface without changing the total mass, so the balance cannot rule it out. Marking the water level on the tumbler settles it: if the level stays at the mark while drops collect outside, no water is seeping out.
s: (a) about 0.43 g per 5 minutes (2.6 g in 30 minutes)
(b) about 489.0 g
(c) not proved, since seepage would not change the total mass; mark the water level to settle it

questions.q: True or False? When drops form on the outside of a covered glass of iced water in a closed room, the air of the room ends up holding slightly less water vapour than before. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The drops are water vapour from the room air that has condensed into liquid on the cold glass. That vapour is no longer in the air, so the amount of water vapour in the air (the humidity) falls slightly.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the drops are vapour taken from the room air and turned into liquid, so less vapour is left in the air

questions.q: On a cold January morning in Delhi, the windows of a crowded school bus are covered with drops on the inside, while the outer side of the glass is dry. It is not raining. Where did the water most likely come from?
questions.a: Water vapour in the air inside the bus condensed on the cold glass
o: Water vapour in the air inside the bus condensed on the cold glass
Water from the cold air outside seeped in through the window glass
Frost formed on the outside of the glass and melted through to the inside
Water evaporated out of the cold glass and settled on its inner side

questions.q:
Kamala boils 500 mL of water in a half-filled pan for 10 minutes on two days. On Monday she leaves the pan uncovered and 440 mL is left. On Tuesday she covers it with a steel plate and 485 mL is left; when she lifts the plate, its inner side is covered with drops.
'Covering the pan saves water.' Justify this statement.
(a) Use the data: how much water was lost each day, and what fraction of Monday's loss did the cover save?
(b) Trace the water that the cover saved, naming each change of state, and say where that water went on Monday.
questions.a: (a) Monday: 500 - 440 = 60 mL lost. Tuesday: 500 - 485 = 15 mL lost. The cover saved 60 - 15 = 45 mL, which is 45/60 = 3/4 of Monday's loss. (b) The boiling water evaporates into water vapour. On Tuesday the vapour rises and touches the cooler steel plate, condenses into drops on its inner side, and the drops run back into the pan, so the water is kept. On Monday nothing stopped the vapour, so it went into the air of the kitchen and was lost from the pan.
s: (a) 60 mL and 15 mL lost
(a) 45 mL saved, which is 3/4 of Monday's loss
(b) boiling water evaporates into vapour
(b) vapour condenses on the cooler plate and the drops return to the pan
(b) uncovered, the vapour escapes into the kitchen air

questions.q: Which observation can be explained ONLY by condensation, with no chance that it is seepage or a leak?
questions.a: Drops forming on the outside of an empty, dry steel bottle just taken out of the freezer
o: Drops forming on the outside of an empty, dry steel bottle just taken out of the freezer
A wet surface forming all over the outside of an unglazed clay pot that is full of water
A wet patch spreading under a plastic jug of water that has a hairline crack in it
Drops forming on the outside of a closed glass tumbler filled to the brim with ice-water

questions.q:
Sana dries a load of wet clothes inside her closed room. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air.
(a) Does drying the clothes change the humidity of the room? Explain.
(b) Later she keeps a cold steel jug in the same room. Why do drops gather on it faster now than they did on the same jug before the clothes were dried there?
questions.a: (a) Yes, it raises it. The water in the clothes evaporates and adds water vapour to the air of the room, so the air holds more water vapour. (b) The drops on the jug are water vapour from the air condensing on its cold surface. The room's air now holds more water vapour, so more of it comes in contact with the cold jug and condenses, and drops gather faster.
s: Part (a): yes, the evaporated water adds vapour to the air, so humidity rises
Part (b): the drops are condensed vapour from the air, and there is more vapour now to condense

questions.q: Dhruv says, 'The drops on the inside of a lid over boiling water and the drops on the outside of a glass of ice water are both formed by condensation, and in both cases the water came from the air of the room.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Both sets of drops are formed by condensation, when water vapour touches a cooler surface. But the source differs: under the lid the vapour comes from the boiling water in the pan itself, while on the glass of ice water it comes from the water vapour in the room air.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: both are condensation of water vapour on a cooler surface
Wrong part: the lid's vapour comes from the boiling water in the pan, not the room air

questions.q:
Amma packs hot idlis into a steel tiffin box and closes the lid at once. At lunchtime the inside of the lid is wet and the top idlis are soggy.
(a) Where did the water on the lid come from? Name the two changes of state in order.
(b) Suggest how Amma could pack the idlis so the lid stays dry, and explain why it works.
questions.a: (a) From the hot idlis. Water in them evaporated into water vapour inside the closed box (evaporation), and when the vapour touched the lid, which had cooled, it changed back into drops (condensation). (b) Let the idlis cool before closing the box. Cool idlis give off much less water vapour, so there is little vapour inside the box to condense on the lid.
s: Part (a): from the idlis: evaporation, then condensation on the cooler lid
Part (b): let them cool first, so much less vapour forms to condense

questions.q:
Two identical covered glass tumblers stand on two digital balances for 30 minutes. Tumbler A holds iced water; tumbler B holds the same amount of water at room temperature. Both have the water level marked.
(a) Predict what you will see on the outside of each tumbler and how each balance reading will change. Explain your predictions.
(b) What does comparing A with B tell you about where the drops come from? Explain why B is needed for this.
questions.a: (a) Drops form on the outside of A, and A's reading increases, because its surface is cold and water vapour from the air condenses on it. B shows no drops (or hardly any) and its reading stays about the same, because its surface is not cold. (b) The two set-ups differ only in how cold they are; the glass, the amount of water and the room are the same. Since only the cold tumbler gains drops and mass while its level stays at the mark, the drops come from water vapour in the air condensing on a cold surface, not from water seeping through the glass. Without B we could not show that coldness, and not the glass itself, is what matters.
s: (a) A: drops form and the reading rises
(a) B: no drops and the reading stays about the same
(a) reason: only A's surface is cold, so vapour condenses on it
(b) only coldness differs, so the drops are condensed vapour from the air
(b) B rules out the glass itself letting water through

questions.q:
In a hostel bathroom, a cold-water pipe and a hot-water pipe run side by side along the wall. On humid days the cold-water pipe is covered with drops that drip onto the floor, while the hot-water pipe stays dry.
(a) Why does only the cold-water pipe drip, though both pipes are in the same air?
(b) The warden wraps the cold-water pipe in a thick cloth cover and the dripping stops. Explain why.
questions.a: (a) Water vapour in the air forms droplets only when it comes in contact with a cold surface. The cold-water pipe is cold, so vapour condenses on it; the hot-water pipe is not cold, so no drops form. (b) The air now touches the outer side of the cloth, which is not cold like the pipe, so the water vapour in the air does not meet a cold surface and does not condense.
s: Part (a): vapour condenses only on a cold surface; only one pipe is cold
Part (b): the air now touches the cloth, which is not cold, so no condensation

questions.q: Write a situation from a kitchen, not about a glass or tumbler of iced water, in which water vapour condenses. Name the cold surface, say where the water vapour comes from, and say what you would see.
questions.a: For example: Amma takes a steel box of curd out of the fridge and keeps it on the counter while the rice is boiling. The cold lid of the box is the cold surface. Water vapour comes from the kitchen air, which also holds vapour from the boiling rice. Within a few minutes tiny droplets appear on the lid, and they join into bigger drops.
s: A kitchen situation with a named cold surface (not an iced-water glass)
Source of the water vapour stated (the air, or steam from cooking)
What is seen: droplets forming, then bigger drops

questions.q:
Pooja fills a glass tumbler and an unglazed clay kulhad with the same amount of iced water, marks the level on each, and weighs each on a balance at the start and after 30 minutes.
Glass: outside wet with drops; level at the mark; mass 450.0 g, then 451.5 g.
Kulhad: outside wet all over; level 3 mm below the mark; mass 450.0 g, then 446.0 g.
(a) Where did the water on the outside of the glass come from?
(b) What does the fall in the kulhad's level show?
(c) The kulhad's outside is wet, yet its mass fell by 4.0 g. Explain where that water went.
(d) Pooja wants to show her class that drops on a cold container can come from the air. Which container should she use, and why not the other?
questions.a: (a) From water vapour in the air, which condensed on the cold glass; the level did not fall and the mass rose by 1.5 g. (b) Water seeped out through the clay wall of the kulhad. (c) The water that seeped through the clay evaporated from the kulhad's outer surface into the air, so the kulhad lost mass even though its outside looked wet. (d) The glass. Its level stays at the mark and its mass rises, so the drops can only have come from the air. In the kulhad seepage and evaporation are mixed in, the level falls and the mass drops, so it cannot show condensation on its own.
s: (a) condensed water vapour from the air (level same, mass up 1.5 g)
(b) water seeped out through the clay
(c) the seeped water evaporated from the outer surface
(d) the glass, since in the kulhad seepage hides the condensation

questions.q:
On a summer afternoon, a box of candle-wax pieces and an open bottle of coconut oil both tip over on a kitchen shelf.
(a) Which spill can be picked up piece by piece, and which needs a cloth to wipe it up? Give the property of each state that decides this.
(b) The same two things tip over on a cold winter morning when the oil in the bottle has set solid. How would the oil spill be different now?
questions.a: (a) The wax pieces can be picked up one by one: wax is a solid, which keeps its own shape and does not flow or spread. The coconut oil needs wiping: in summer it is a liquid, which flows and spreads over the shelf. (b) The solid oil would not flow out of the bottle or spread; it would stay as a lump that keeps its shape, like the wax pieces, until it is warmed and melts.
s: Part (a): wax is a solid (keeps shape, does not flow); the oil is a liquid (flows and spreads)
Part (b): solid oil keeps its shape and does not flow or spread out

questions.q: Ravi tips ten small pebbles from a square box into a round bowl, and pours a cup of milk from a jug onto a flat plate. Which prediction is correct?
questions.a: Each pebble keeps its own shape; the milk takes the plate's shape and keeps its volume
o: Each pebble keeps its own shape; the milk takes the plate's shape and keeps its volume
The pebbles flow into the bowl's round shape, just as the milk takes the plate's shape
Each pebble becomes rounder in the bowl, while the milk keeps the shape of the jug
Each pebble keeps its shape, and the milk's volume grows as it spreads on the plate

questions.q:
Read the statements about the states of water.
Statement 1: Ice does not flow, but it spreads out when it is placed on a flat surface.
Statement 2: Water spreads on a surface while its volume stays the same.
Statement 3: Water vapour keeps a fixed shape, just as ice does.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
A frozen kulfi stands upright on its stick and keeps its cone shape. Left on a plate in the sun, it drips and then lies as a pool shaped like the plate.
(a) Which property of each state does the kulfi show, frozen and then melted?
(b) Is the melted kulfi a different substance from the frozen one? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Frozen, it is a solid and keeps its own shape. Melted, it is a liquid: it flows and takes the shape of the plate. (b) No. It is the same substance in a different state, just as ice and water are two states of one substance; only heating changed its state.
s: Part (a): solid keeps its shape; liquid flows and takes the shape of the plate
Part (b): same substance, only its state has changed

questions.q: Manoj pours 300 mL of water from a tall bottle into a wide, flat tray. Which statement about the water in the tray is correct?
questions.a: Its shape changes, but its volume stays 300 mL
o: Its shape changes, but its volume stays 300 mL
Its shape and its volume both change in the tray
Its volume grows, because it has spread out more
Its shape stays the same, but its volume falls

questions.q: Jalebis are being fried in the kitchen, and Grandpa smells them while sitting in the drawing room. Which property explains how the smell reached him?
questions.a: A gas spreads out through all the space available to it
o: A gas spreads out through all the space available to it
A gas keeps a fixed shape and travels in a straight line
A liquid flows along the floor from room to room
A solid keeps its shape, so the smell stays in the jalebis

questions.q: True or False? Water vapour, like liquid water, has no fixed shape, but unlike liquid water it does not keep a fixed volume when it spreads. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Liquid water takes the shape of its container and spreads while its volume stays constant. Water vapour also has no fixed shape, but it spreads out into the entire space available to it, so it has no fixed volume.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: water spreads keeping its volume constant; vapour spreads into all the available space

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Water poured from a jug onto a plate takes the shape of the plate.
Reason (R): The volume of water stays the same when it is poured from one container into another.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
In a class activity, students move an ice cube (2 cm on each side) from a square steel bowl into a round glass dish. Then they pour 150 mL of water into a tall glass, where it stands 12 cm high, and from there onto a flat plate, where it spreads into a pool about 1 cm deep.
(a) What happens to the shape of the ice cube in the round dish, and why?
(b) Why did the same water stand 12 cm high in the glass but only about 1 cm deep on the plate?
(c) Tara wants star-shaped ice for a party. She can pour water into a star-shaped mould and freeze it, or freeze a plain block of ice and carve a star out of it. Which would you advise? Use the properties of the two states.
questions.a: (a) It keeps its cube shape, because a solid retains its shape whatever container it is in. (b) Water has no fixed shape: it takes the shape of each container and spreads on the plate, while its volume stays 150 mL, so it is tall and narrow in the glass and wide and shallow on the plate. (c) Freeze water in the mould. As a liquid, the water flows into every point of the star and takes the mould's shape; once frozen, the solid keeps that shape. A block of ice keeps its own block shape, so a star could be got only by cutting it away bit by bit.
s: (a) the cube keeps its shape, as a solid does
(b) water takes each container's shape while its volume stays the same
(c) freeze in the mould: the liquid fills the shape and the solid then keeps it

questions.q: Gita says, 'Solid, liquid and gas are states only water can have; every other substance is always just a solid or always just a liquid.' Which observation shows she is wrong?
questions.a: Ghee is firm in a jar in winter but runs freely when warmed in a pan
o: Ghee is firm in a jar in winter but runs freely when warmed in a pan
Stones, wood and glass keep their own shape in any container
Milk and oil take the shape of whatever vessel they are poured into
Oxygen and carbon dioxide spread through all the air of a room

questions.q:
On a January morning in a Shimla kitchen, Dolma notices: the ghee in a jar is firm and pale; a spoonful of the same ghee warmed in a pan runs freely; a candle on the shelf is solid, but the wax near its burning wick is runny; and steam rises from the pressure cooker and soon reaches every corner of the kitchen.
(a) Which two substances, other than water, are seen in two different states?
(b) Describe a simple test Dolma could do with the jar to show that its ghee is in the solid state.
(c) Which state of water is the steam, and which property does it show?
(d) A recipe card in Dolma's house says 'ghee: a liquid'. Is this a fair description? Give a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: (a) Ghee (firm in the jar, runny when warmed) and candle wax (solid candle, runny near the flame). (b) Tip the jar: if the ghee keeps its own shape and does not flow towards the mouth of the jar, it is a solid. (c) The gaseous state, water vapour (made visible by tiny droplets); it spreads out into all the available space. (d) Only partly fair: ghee is a solid or a liquid depending on whether it is cooled or heated, as the kitchen shows, so 'liquid' is true only when it is warm.
s: (a) ghee and candle wax
(b) tipping test: keeps its shape and does not flow
(c) gaseous state, spreads into all available space
(d) partly fair: its state depends on heating or cooling

questions.q: Meena pours 600 mL of water equally into three glasses of very different shapes: one tall and thin, one short and wide, and one shaped like a cone. She then pours all the water from the cone-shaped glass into a flat dish, without spilling. The dish now holds ___ mL of water.

Ms Rao rubs a few drops of scented sanitiser on her hands at the front of a closed classroom. A minute later, students on the last bench can smell it.
(a) In which state did the sanitiser reach the last bench?
(b) Which property of that state explains this, and why could the liquid sanitiser not do it?
questions.a: (a) As a gas (vapour), after the sanitiser evaporated from her hands. (b) A gas spreads out into all the space available to it, so it spread through the whole room to the back benches. A liquid only flows and spreads over a surface while keeping its volume, so it would have stayed on her hands.
s: Part (a): as a gas, after evaporating
Part (b): a gas spreads into all available space; a liquid keeps its volume and stays on the surface

questions.q: Kiran says, 'The steam rising from the pressure cooker and the invisible water vapour that leaves wet clothes on the line are the same state of water.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. Both are water in its gaseous state, water vapour. Water vapour itself is invisible; the steam above the cooker can be seen only because part of it has turned into tiny water droplets, while the vapour from the clothes has not, so it cannot be seen.
s: Verdict: Yes, the claim is correct
Both are the gaseous state of water, water vapour
Steam is visible only because of tiny droplets; the vapour itself is invisible

questions.q: In a class test, four unknown substances are each tipped from a cup into a flat dish. Which result shows that a substance is in the solid state?
questions.a: It drops out in one piece with the cup's shape and stays that way in the dish
o: It drops out in one piece with the cup's shape and stays that way in the dish
It oozes out very slowly and then settles into the round shape of the dish
It flows out quickly and spreads over the dish as a thin, wide layer
Nothing seems to come out, but its smell soon reaches every corner of the room

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I
1. An ice cube
2. Water in a glass
3. Water vapour in a room
4. Ghee in a jar on a cold winter morning
Column II
a. No fixed shape, spreads into all the space, cannot be seen
b. Keeps its own shape and does not flow (state of water)
c. No fixed shape, but its volume stays the same when poured
d. A substance other than water, in its solid state

A classroom has no visible water anywhere, yet drops form all round a glass of iced water placed on the teacher's table.
(a) In which state was the water that formed the drops, and why could nobody see it beforehand?
(b) Why did the drops form all round the glass, not just on the side facing a window?
questions.a: (a) In the gaseous state, as water vapour in the air; water vapour is invisible. (b) Water vapour spreads out into the entire available space, so it was present in the air on every side of the glass and condensed all round its cold surface.
s: Part (a): water vapour (gas), which is invisible
Part (b): vapour fills all the available space, so it surrounds the glass

questions.q:
Kabir writes five conclusions in his notebook. Say whether each is correct or wrong, giving the property of the state that decides it.
(i) Coconut oil that has set white in its bottle on a winter morning does not move when the bottle is tipped, so at that time it is a solid.
(ii) Honey moves very slowly when the jar is tipped, so honey is a solid.
(iii) A litre of water poured on the floor spreads into a big puddle, so its volume has increased.
(iv) The smell of an agarbatti lit in one corner reaches every corner of the room, so the smell travels through the air as a gas.
(v) An ice cube in a round glass of lemonade takes the round shape of the glass after a few minutes, so ice changes its shape to fit its container.
questions.a: (i) Correct: it keeps its own shape and does not flow, which is how a solid behaves; coconut oil sets solid in winter. (ii) Wrong: honey does flow, only slowly, and it takes the shape of its jar, so it is a liquid. (iii) Wrong: water spreads while its volume stays constant; only its shape changes. (iv) Correct: a gas spreads out into the entire space available, which is how the smell reaches every corner. (v) Wrong: ice keeps its own shape in any container; what fits the glass is the water from the part of the ice that has melted, a change of state.
s: (i) correct: keeps its shape and does not flow, so solid
(ii) wrong: honey flows (slowly) and takes its container's shape, so liquid
(iii) wrong: water spreads with its volume constant
(iv) correct: a gas spreads into all the available space
(v) wrong: ice keeps its shape; only melted water takes the glass's shape

questions.q: Show that the water vapour from a cup of water cannot be kept in an open cup in the way the water itself is kept.
questions.a: Liquid water has a constant volume and takes the shape of the cup, so the walls and bottom of the cup hold it. Water vapour has no fixed shape and no fixed volume: it spreads out into the entire space available to it. An open cup has no lid, so the vapour spreads out of the top into the room, and the cup cannot hold it.
s: Water keeps a fixed volume, so the cup's walls and base hold it
Vapour spreads into all the available space
So it escapes from the open top into the room

questions.q: Dev says, 'An ice cube must really be a liquid, because it melts as soon as it is put in a drink. Calling it a solid is wrong.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. While it is frozen the ice cube keeps its own shape, does not flow and does not spread, so it is in the solid state. Melting is a change of state: when heat is supplied, the solid changes into a liquid. Being able to melt shows only that its state can change, not that it was a liquid all along.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Frozen ice keeps its shape and does not flow: solid state
Melting is a change of state on heating, not proof that it was a liquid

questions.q:
Three friends look at the ice in their lemonade.
Anu: 'Ice is hard and water is not, so they are different substances.'
Bala: 'Water left in the freezer becomes ice, but something must get added to it in the freezer.'
Chitra: 'Ice and water are the same substance.'
(a) Who is right? Explain what is wrong with the reasoning of each of the other two.
(b) Design a simple test, using a covered steel tumbler, a freezer and a digital weighing balance, that would show Bala nothing is added in the freezer. Say what result you expect.
questions.a: (a) Chitra is right: ice and water are two states (forms) of the same substance. Anu mistakes a difference in behaviour for a difference in substance: ice is the solid state, which keeps its shape, and water is the liquid state, which flows and splashes. Bala's idea fails because when the ice is taken out of the freezer it simply melts and is converted back into water; the freezer only cools the water. (b) Weigh a covered steel tumbler of water, put it in the freezer until the water has frozen, take it out, and let all the ice melt with the cover still on. When the tumbler is back at room temperature, wipe its outside dry (to remove any drops condensed from the air) and weigh it again. The two readings are the same, so nothing was added in the freezer: the water was only cooled into ice and warmed back.
s: (a) Chitra, with ice and water as two states of one substance
(a) Anu: different behaviour means a different state, not a different substance
(a) Bala: the freezer only cools; taken out, the ice melts back into water
(b) a fair test: weigh the covered water before freezing and again after it melts back, with the outside wiped dry
(b) expected result: the same mass, so nothing was added

questions.q:
In late February in Pune, Arun keeps a bottle of coconut oil on the kitchen window sill. Each day at 1 p.m., just before lunch, he notes the kitchen temperature and the state of the oil.
Monday 23 degrees C: solid. Tuesday 22 degrees C: solid. Wednesday 28 degrees C: runny. Thursday 24 degrees C: solid. Friday 29 degrees C: runny.
(a) What pattern links the state of the oil to the temperature?
(b) Name the change that happened to the oil between Wednesday and Thursday, and say what caused it.
(c) Arun can keep the bottle on the sill or on a shelf just above the fridge, where his thermometer reads about 31 degrees C at 1 p.m. every day. Where should he keep it if he wants the oil to pour at lunchtime every day? Use the data.
questions.a: (a) The oil was liquid on the warmer days (28 and 29 degrees C) and solid on the cooler ones (24 degrees C and below). (b) Freezing: the kitchen became cooler, the oil lost heat and the liquid oil turned solid. (c) On the shelf above the fridge. At about 31 degrees C every day it is warmer than 28 and 29 degrees C, the temperatures at which the oil was already runny, so it should stay liquid; on the sill it was solid on every day of 24 degrees C or below.
s: (a) liquid on the warmer days, solid on the cooler ones
(b) freezing, as the oil lost heat to the cooler kitchen
(c) the shelf, since 31 degrees C is above the 28-29 degrees C at which the oil was runny

questions.q: On a winter day in Delhi, the coconut oil in Meenu's bottle is solid at 7 a.m., runny by 2 p.m., and solid again the next morning. Which describes the two changes, in order, from 7 a.m. to the next morning?
questions.a: Melting as the oil gained heat, then freezing as it lost heat
o: Melting as the oil gained heat, then freezing as it lost heat
Freezing as the oil gained heat, then melting as it lost heat
Melting as the oil lost heat, then freezing as it gained heat
Evaporation during the day, then condensation during the night

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To change water into ice, we must supply heat to the water.
Reason (R): To change ice into water, heat must be supplied to the ice.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Vivek puts one ice cube on a steel plate in the sun and an identical cube on a steel plate in the shade, side by side on the terrace.
(a) Which cube melts first, and why?
(b) The cube in the shade melts too, though no sunlight falls on it. Where does its heat come from?
questions.a: (a) The cube in the sun, because the sun supplies more heat to it, and supplying heat melts ice. (b) From its warmer surroundings: the air around it and the plate it rests on.
s: Part (a): the sunny cube, as more heat is supplied to it
Part (b): heat from the warmer air and plate around it

questions.q: For a class demonstration, Rani needs a steel bowl of ice cubes turned into water within a few minutes. What should she do?
questions.a: Keep the steel bowl of ice cubes over gentle heat
o: Keep the steel bowl of ice cubes over gentle heat
Put the bowl into the freezer for a little while
Wrap the bowl tightly in a cold, wet cloth
Add some more ice cubes to the same bowl

questions.q: A school freezer removes enough heat to freeze 1.5 L of water into ice every 2 hours. To freeze 6 L of water for the sports-day ice box, working at the same rate, it needs ___ hours.
On a January night in Srinagar, the water in an outdoor pipe freezes, and in the morning no water comes out of the tap. Which action will get the water flowing again soonest?
questions.a: Wrapping the pipe in a cloth soaked in warm water
o: Wrapping the pipe in a cloth soaked in warm water
Opening the tap fully so that the ice can flow out
Pouring a bucket of cold water over the frozen pipe
Waiting until the evening, when the air is colder

questions.q:
At a Diwali workshop, children heat old candle wax in a pan until it is runny, pour it into clay diyas with a wick in the middle, and leave the diyas on a table to set. Some wax drips onto the table.
(a) Name the two changes of state the wax goes through, and say whether heat is supplied or removed in each.
(b) Why must the wax be poured while it is runny and not after it has set?
(c) Should the children scrape the dripped wax off at once, or wait? Give a reason.
(d) One pan was left on the warm stove after the flame was turned off, and its wax stayed runny much longer than the wax in a pan placed on the cool floor. Explain.
questions.a: (a) Melting in the pan, where heat is supplied; freezing in the diyas, where heat is removed as the wax cools. (b) Runny wax is a liquid: it flows and takes the shape of the diya. Once set, it is a solid that keeps its own shape, so it cannot be poured. (c) Wait. While runny it would spread and smear; once it has cooled and frozen into a solid it keeps its shape and can be lifted off in one piece. (d) The warm stove slowed the loss of heat from the wax, so it stayed liquid longer; on the cool floor heat was removed faster, so the wax froze sooner.
s: (a) melting with heat supplied, freezing with heat removed
(b) liquid wax takes the diya's shape; set wax keeps its own shape
(c) wait until it freezes solid, then lift it off
(d) the warm stove slowed the loss of heat, so freezing was delayed

questions.q: Sneha says, 'To turn ice into water vapour we must supply heat, and to turn that water vapour back into ice we must supply even more heat.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is correct: heat is supplied to change ice into water and water into water vapour. The second part is wrong: going back needs cooling, not more heat. The water vapour must be cooled (for example by meeting a cold surface) to condense into water, and the water must then be cooled in a freezer, where heat is removed, to freeze into ice.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: heat is supplied for ice to water to vapour
Wrong part: going back needs cooling (cold surface, then freezer), not more heat

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: An ice cream softening in a bowl is melting, because it gains heat from its surroundings.
Statement 2: Water placed in a freezer turns into ice because heat is supplied to it there.
Statement 3: Candle wax can only melt; once it is liquid it cannot become solid again.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Anya warms solid ghee in a pan until it is completely runny, pours it into a small star-shaped steel mould and leaves it on a cool window sill. An hour later the ghee is firm, and she tips the star out onto a plate.
(a) Name the change in the pan and the change on the sill, saying whether heat is supplied or removed in each.
(b) Will the ghee star keep its shape on the plate in the cool room? What would happen if she put it in a hot pan instead? Give reasons.
questions.a: (a) In the pan the solid ghee melts, because heat is supplied; on the sill the liquid ghee freezes, because heat is removed as it cools. (b) In the cool room it keeps its star shape, because it is a solid and a solid keeps its own shape. In a hot pan heat is supplied, so it would melt into a liquid and spread out to take the shape of the pan.
s: Part (a): melting with heat supplied, then freezing with heat removed
Part (b): keeps its shape as a solid when cool; in a hot pan it melts and takes the pan's shape

questions.q: After a festival lunch, four pairs of changes are noticed in the kitchen. Which pair shows two OPPOSITE changes of state of the same substance?
questions.a: Ghee melting in a hot pan, and leftover ghee setting firm in a cold bowl
o: Ghee melting in a hot pan, and leftover ghee setting firm in a cold bowl
Butter softening on a hot paratha, and ghee setting firm in a cold bowl
Ice melting in a glass of water, and drops forming outside a cold bottle
Water freezing in an ice tray, and a wet dupatta drying on the balcony

questions.q: True or False? Coconut oil that has turned solid in its bottle on a winter night is no longer oil; it has changed into a different substance. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The oil has only changed its state: it lost heat to the cold surroundings and froze into solid oil. It is still the same substance, and supplying heat (for example, standing the bottle in warm water) melts it back into liquid oil.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: only its state changed on cooling; heating melts it back into liquid oil

questions.q:
Match each kitchen event in Column I with the change it shows in Column II.
Column I
1. Melted ghee in a steel bowl setting firm on a winter night
2. Ice in a kulfi box turning to water at a fair
3. A mopped kitchen floor becoming dry without any heating
4. A cool lid over boiling dal becoming wet on its inner side
Column II
a. Heat supplied; a solid changes into a liquid
b. Heat removed; a liquid changes into a solid
c. Water vapour touching a cold surface changes into a liquid
d. A liquid changes into vapour, even at room temperature

Three identical steel cups, each holding 50 mL of runny candle wax just poured from the same pan, are left to set at the same time: cup P on a shelf inside the fridge, cup Q on the kitchen table, and cup R on a shelf beside an oven that is switched on. The wax in P is solid after 12 minutes and in Q after 30 minutes; the wax in R is still runny after 2 hours.
(a) How many times as long did the wax in Q take to set as the wax in P?
(b) Explain the difference between P and Q using heat.
(c) Explain why the wax in R did not set.
questions.a: (a) 30 / 12 = 2.5 times as long. (b) Freezing needs heat to be removed. The fridge is a much colder place, so heat is removed from P faster and its wax freezes sooner; on the table heat is removed more slowly, so Q takes longer. (c) Beside the hot oven the cup keeps getting heat from its surroundings, so heat is not removed from the wax and the liquid cannot freeze into a solid.
s: (a) 2.5 times
(b) heat is removed faster in the fridge, so the wax freezes sooner
(c) beside the oven heat is supplied, not removed, so it stays liquid

questions.q: Rahul moves a tray of ice cubes from the freezer to the lower shelf of the fridge, which is cold but not as cold as the freezer. A few hours later the ice has turned into water. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: The ice gained heat from the shelf, which is warmer than the ice
o: The ice gained heat from the shelf, which is warmer than the ice
The ice lost heat to the shelf, and losing heat makes ice melt
Nothing supplied heat; ice turns to water by itself in any fridge
The fridge supplied coldness to the ice, and coldness melts ice

questions.q: At a wedding, the cook must (a) turn a 2 kg block of ice into water for sharbat as quickly as possible, and later (b) turn the leftover sharbat into ice lollies for the children. For each job, say whether heat must be supplied or removed, and how he can do it in the kitchen.
questions.a: (a) Heat must be supplied: break the block into pieces and keep them in a steel vessel over gentle heat (or in a warm place) so the ice melts quickly. (b) Heat must be removed: pour the sharbat into moulds and keep them in the freezer, where it is cold, so it freezes.
s: Part (a): supply heat, e.g. a steel vessel over gentle heat
Part (b): remove heat, e.g. moulds in the freezer

questions.q:
Follow some water on its journey through a kitchen.
(i) Water in an ice tray in the freezer becomes ice.
(ii) The ice cubes are put into a glass on the table and become water.
(iii) That water is boiled in a kettle and turns into steam.
(iv) Some steam touches a cool steel lid and forms drops.
(v) The drops are collected and put back in the freezer, where they become ice again.
(a) Name the change of state at each of the five steps.
(b) For steps (i), (ii), (iii) and (v), say whether heat is supplied or removed.
(c) Step (iv) needs neither a stove nor a freezer. What does it need instead?
questions.a: (a) (i) freezing; (ii) melting; (iii) water to water vapour, evaporation (as steam); (iv) condensation; (v) freezing. (b) (i) heat removed; (ii) heat supplied, from the warmer surroundings; (iii) heat supplied; (v) heat removed. (c) A cold surface: water vapour forms droplets when it comes in contact with a cold surface, here the cool steel lid.
s: (a) freezing, melting, evaporation, condensation, freezing
(b) removed, supplied, supplied, removed
(c) a cold surface for the vapour to touch

questions.q:
In Leh in winter, a bucket of water left in the courtyard overnight has a layer of ice on top in the morning.
(a) Name the change and say what took heat away from the water.
(b) Tashi's cousin says only a freezer can make ice. Use the bucket to correct him.
questions.a: (a) Freezing; the cold surroundings (the cold night air) took heat away from the water. (b) A freezer is only one cold environment. Any liquid freezes when enough heat is removed from it, as the bucket left out on a freezing night shows.
s: Part (a): freezing, heat removed by the cold surroundings
Part (b): any cold enough place removes heat and freezes water, not only a freezer

questions.q: Write a short real-life situation, using a substance other than water or candle wax, in which a person melts the substance and then lets it freeze on purpose. Name the substance, say how heat is supplied, and say how heat is removed.
questions.a: For example: before Pongal, Kavya's grandmother keeps a tin of solid ghee in a pan of hot water (heat supplied) until the ghee melts. She pours the liquid ghee into small steel cups to give to neighbours, and leaves the cups on the cool window sill, where the ghee loses heat and freezes into firm ghee in the shape of the cups.
s: A realistic situation with a substance other than water or wax
How heat is supplied to melt it
How heat is removed so it freezes

questions.q:
For the school fair, Class 6 makes 40 ice lollies, each from 60 mL of mango drink poured into a mould. The school freezer needs 6 hours to freeze them. The fair opens at 9 a.m. The class can fill the moulds at 4 p.m. the day before or at 5 a.m. on the fair day. On the fair day they test one lolly on the counter: in the sun near the gate it melts completely in 15 minutes; at a shaded corner it takes 30 minutes.
(a) Why must the filled moulds go into the freezer, and what change happens to the mango drink there?
(b) How many times as long does a lolly last in the shade as in the sun, and why does the sun make it melt faster?
(c) When should the class fill the moulds, and where should the lolly box be kept during the fair? Use the data for both.
questions.a: (a) To turn a liquid into a solid, heat must be removed from it. The freezer is a cold place that removes heat from the drink, so the liquid drink freezes into a solid lolly. (b) 30 / 15 = 2 times as long; in the sun more heat is supplied to the lolly, so it melts faster. (c) Fill the moulds at 4 p.m. the day before: they are frozen by 10 p.m. Filled at 5 a.m. they would be ready only at 11 a.m., two hours after the fair opens. Keep the lolly box at the shaded corner, where less heat reaches the lollies and each lasts twice as long.
s: (a) heat must be removed; in the freezer the liquid drink freezes into a solid
(b) 2 times; the sun supplies more heat
(c) fill at 4 p.m. (5 a.m. + 6 h = 11 a.m. is too late); keep the box in the shade

questions.q:
Each set-up below holds 5 mL of water, and the four were tried on different days. Match each set-up in Column I with its drying time in Column II.
Column I
1. Spread on a plate, in the sun, with a breeze, dry day
2. Spread on a plate, in the shade, still air, dry day

Column II
a. 300 minutes
b. 20 minutes
c. 150 minutes
d. 45 minutes
Harsh pours 10 mL of water into a small steel katori and another 10 mL onto a wide thali, and keeps them side by side on the window sill. Which will dry first, and why?
questions.a: The thali, because more of its water is exposed to the air
o: The thali, because more of its water is exposed to the air
The katori, because its water is deeper and holds more heat
Both together, because they hold the same amount of water
The katori, because steel takes in water faster than a thali

questions.q:
Nani dries washed red chillies on the terrace.
(a) Why does she spread them out in a single layer instead of leaving them in a heap?
(b) Why does she bring them in when the evening air turns damp?
questions.a: (a) Spread out, more of their wet surface is exposed to the air; a larger exposed area makes water evaporate faster. (b) Damp evening air already holds a lot of water vapour (high humidity), and when there is more water vapour in the air, water evaporates slowly, so the chillies would stop drying.
s: Part (a): a larger exposed area speeds up evaporation
Part (b): damp air is humid, and high humidity slows evaporation

questions.q: Identical bottle caps, each with 5 mL of water, are set out on the same dry day. In the shade with still air the water takes 75 minutes to evaporate; in the sun with still air, 40 minutes; in the sun with a breeze, 25 minutes. Which conclusion do these results support?
questions.a: Both sunlight and moving air speed up evaporation
o: Both sunlight and moving air speed up evaporation
Only sunlight affects how fast water evaporates
Moving air slows down evaporation in the sun
Water evaporates fastest in still air in the shade

questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
