questions.q: During the monsoon, Arjun's washed uniform hangs under a shed all day and is still damp in the evening, though no rain fell on it. Which reason best explains this?
questions.a: The air already holds a lot of water vapour, so evaporation is slow
o: The air already holds a lot of water vapour, so evaporation is slow
Rainy air is so cold that the water in the cloth freezes
The shed stops all the air from touching the uniform
Water can evaporate only in direct sunlight, never under a roof or shed

questions.q:
Students put 5 mL of water in each of four set-ups and recorded the time for it to evaporate completely.
A: bottle cap, shade, still air: 150 minutes.
B: plate, shade, still air: 40 minutes.
C: bottle cap, sunlight, still air: 70 minutes.
D: bottle cap, shade, in front of a fan: 90 minutes.
(a) How many times as fast did the water evaporate in B as in A?
(b) Which two set-ups show the effect of sunlight alone?
(c) How many times as fast did the fan make the water evaporate, compared with still air? Give your answer to two decimal places.
(d) On a cloudy day, the hostel warden can either spread the wet bedsheets out fully in a still room, or fold each one small and hang it in front of a fan. Folding cuts the exposed area about as much as going from a plate to a bottle cap. Using the data, which would you advise?
questions.a: (a) 150 / 40 = 3.75 times as fast. (b) A and C, which differ only in sunlight. (c) 150 / 90 = 1.67 times as fast. (d) Spread them out fully. Spread sheets in still air are like set-up B (large area, still air: 40 minutes); folded sheets in front of a fan are like set-up D (small area, fan: 90 minutes). The large exposed area helped far more than the fan, so spreading dries the sheets faster.
s: (a) 3.75 times
(b) A and C
(c) 1.67 times
(d) spreading advised, by comparing B (40 minutes) with D (90 minutes)

questions.q: 5 mL of water in a bottle cap takes 120 minutes to evaporate, while 5 mL spread on a plate beside it takes 30 minutes. The water on the plate evaporated ___ times as fast.

On the same June day, identical loads of washing dry in 1 hour in Jaisalmer (hot, dry and windy) but take 5 hours in Mumbai (warm, rainy, humid and still).
(a) How many times as long did the washing take in Mumbai?
(b) Name two of the three conditions that explain the difference, saying which way each works.
questions.a: (a) 5 / 1 = 5 times as long. (b) Any two of these three. Humidity: Mumbai's air already holds a lot of water vapour, which slows evaporation. Air movement: Jaisalmer's wind speeds up evaporation, while Mumbai's air is still. Temperature: Jaisalmer's greater heat speeds up evaporation.
s: Part (a): 5 times as long
Part (b): any two of humidity (slows Mumbai), wind (speeds Jaisalmer) and heat (speeds Jaisalmer), each with its direction

questions.q: Sita dries the same sari, spread out, on the same terrace. On three dry (not humid) days it took: hot and still, 2 hours; cool and windy, 3 hours; hot and windy, 1.5 hours. Tomorrow will be dry, cool and completely still. Which is the best estimate of the drying time?
questions.a: More than 3 hours
o: More than 3 hours
Between 2 and 3 hours
Between 1.5 and 2 hours
Less than 1.5 hours

questions.q: True or False? On a humid, rainy day, switching on a fan in the room can make wet clothes dry faster. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. Humidity slows evaporation, but increasing the movement of air makes water evaporate faster, so the fan helps the clothes dry sooner than they would in still air.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: more air movement speeds up evaporation even when humidity slows it

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'Only the sun matters for drying. A wet dupatta will dry just as fast bunched up as spread out, as long as it is in the sun.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. Sunlight does speed up evaporation, but it is not the only condition. A larger exposed area also makes water evaporate faster: spread out, more of the dupatta's water is exposed to the air, so it dries sooner than when bunched up, even in the same sun.
s: Verdict: No, the claim is wrong
Sunlight helps but is not the only condition
Spreading increases the exposed area, so it dries faster

questions.q:
Read the statements about how fast water evaporates.
Statement 1: Water spread on a plate evaporates faster than the same amount in a bottle cap, because a larger area is exposed to the air.
Statement 2: A cap of water kept in sunlight dries faster than an identical cap kept in the shade.
Statement 3: Clothes dry faster on a windy day than on a still day, other things being the same.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements
o: All three statements
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only

questions.q:
A puddle of the same size in the same courtyard takes 6 hours to dry on a still, dry December day and 2 hours on a still, dry May day.
(a) Which condition is mainly responsible for the difference?
(b) Would the December puddle dry sooner or later on a windy December day? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Temperature: May is much hotter, and water evaporates faster in the heat and sunlight. (b) Sooner: with more movement of air, water evaporates faster, even though it is still December.
s: Part (a): the higher temperature in May
Part (b): sooner, because moving air speeds evaporation

questions.q: The classroom floor has just been mopped. Which step would NOT help it dry faster?
questions.a: Switching off the fans and keeping the room still
o: Switching off the fans and keeping the room still
Switching on all the ceiling fans in the classroom at full speed
Spreading the puddles thin with a dry mop
Opening the curtains to let the sunlight in

questions.q: Rohan says, 'When water evaporates it needs heat, and a fan only blows cool air. So drying wet clothes under a fan cannot help at all.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Warmth does speed up evaporation, but it is not the only condition. A fan increases the movement of air, and with more movement of air, water evaporates faster. So clothes under a fan dry sooner than in still air, even though the fan does not warm them.
s: Verdict: No, the conclusion is wrong
Warmth helps, but it is not the only condition
The fan increases air movement, which speeds up evaporation

questions.q:
Ravi comes home in the rain with a wet umbrella.
(a) Why will it dry faster if he leaves it open than if he leaves it folded?
(b) Why will it dry faster still if he leaves it open on a breezy verandah rather than in a closed room?
questions.a: (a) Open, the wet cloth is spread out, so a larger area of it is exposed to the air, and a larger exposed area makes water evaporate faster. (b) On the breezy verandah the air keeps moving over the cloth, and more movement of air makes water evaporate faster.
s: Part (a): opening increases the exposed area
Part (b): moving air speeds up evaporation

questions.q:
A wet towel holding 300 g of water is dried in four different ways on different days.
P: spread out, in the sun, breezy: dry in 1.5 hours.
Q: spread out, in the sun, still air: dry in 2 hours.
R: folded in four, in the sun, still air: dry in 4 hours.
S: spread out, in the shade, rainy and humid: dry in 6 hours.
(a) Find how many grams of water evaporated per hour, on average, in each way, and rank the four ways from fastest to slowest.
(b) Which pair shows the effect of air movement, and which pair the effect of exposed area?
(c) Why can S not be used on its own to find the effect of humidity?
questions.a: (a) P 300/1.5 = 200 g per hour; Q 300/2 = 150 g per hour; R 300/4 = 75 g per hour; S 300/6 = 50 g per hour. Fastest to slowest: P, Q, R, S. (b) Air movement: P and Q (only the breeze differs). Exposed area: Q and R (only spread versus folded differs). (c) S differs from the others in more than one condition, shade as well as rain and humidity, so its slow drying cannot be put down to humidity alone.
s: (a) 200, 150, 75 and 50 g per hour
(a) ranking P, Q, R, S
(b) P and Q for air movement
(b) Q and R for exposed area
(c) S changes more than one condition at once

questions.q: Kunal puts 5 mL of water in a bottle cap in the sun and 5 mL on a plate in the shade. The plate dries first, and he concludes that shade makes water evaporate faster than sunlight. Show that his test cannot support this conclusion.
questions.a: Two conditions differ between the set-ups: the place (sun versus shade) and the exposed area (cap versus plate). The plate's larger exposed area speeds up evaporation, so its faster drying could be due to the area and not the shade. To test sunlight he must change only that: identical caps with equal water, one in the sun, one in the shade.
s: Two conditions were changed at once: sunlight and exposed area
The larger area of the plate can explain the faster drying
A fair test changes only sunlight, keeping identical caps and amounts

questions.q:
Shabana dries the same set of school uniforms on the terrace every day for a week and notes the weather and the drying time.
Monday, hot and sunny, still air: 2 hours.
Tuesday, cloudy and windy: 3 hours.
Wednesday, rainy and humid: 7 hours.
Thursday, hot, sunny and windy: 1.5 hours.
(a) Which condition explains why Wednesday was the slowest?
(b) How many times as long did the uniforms take on Wednesday as on Thursday? Give your answer to one decimal place.
(c) Monday and Thursday were both hot and sunny. What made Thursday faster?
(d) Next Wednesday is again rainy, and the uniforms must be dry by morning. Suggest what she should do and why it should work.
questions.a: (a) High humidity: on a rainy day the air already holds a lot of water vapour, so water evaporates slowly. (b) 7 / 1.5 = 4.7 times as long. (c) The wind: more movement of air makes water evaporate faster. (d) Hang the uniforms spread out (a larger exposed area) indoors under a running fan (more air movement); these two conditions speed up evaporation even when humidity slows it.
s: (a) high humidity
(b) about 4.7 times
(c) air movement (wind)
(d) spread out and use a fan, with reasons

questions.q:
Neha repeats Activity 8.8 on three days with the same air temperature, using identical caps with 5 mL of water each, and records the time for the water to evaporate completely.
Day 1, dry and still: cap in the sun 40 minutes; cap in the shade 70 minutes.
Day 2, dry and windy: cap in the shade 45 minutes.
Day 3, rainy, humid and still: cap in the shade 150 minutes.
(a) On Day 1, how many times as fast did the water evaporate in the sun as in the shade?
(b) Which two caps show the effect of wind alone, and how many minutes did the wind save?
(c) Which shortened the time of a shaded, still cap more: the sun (Day 1) or the wind (Day 2)? Show your working.
(d) Explain the result for Day 3.
questions.a: (a) 70 / 40 = 1.75 times as fast. (b) The shade caps of Day 1 and Day 2, which differ only in air movement: the wind saved 70 - 45 = 25 minutes. (c) The sun saved 70 - 40 = 30 minutes, the wind 25 minutes, so on these days the sun shortened the time slightly more. (d) The air on a rainy day already holds a lot of water vapour (high humidity), so water evaporates slowly: 150 minutes, more than twice the 70 minutes of the dry, still Day 1.
s: (a) 1.75 times as fast
(b) Day 1 and Day 2 shade caps; 25 minutes saved
(c) sun 30 minutes against wind 25 minutes
(c) conclusion: the sun had the larger effect here
(d) high humidity slows evaporation

questions.q:
On a cloudy day Meera asks, 'If clouds are made of water, why does the water float up there, and why does it fall only sometimes?'
(a) Why do cloud droplets float instead of falling at once?
(b) What must happen to the droplets before rain falls?
questions.a: (a) The droplets in a cloud are very small, so they float in the air. (b) Many droplets must join together to form bigger drops of water; only when some drops get so heavy do they start falling as rain.
s: Part (a): cloud droplets are tiny, so they float in the air
Part (b): droplets join into bigger, heavy drops, which then fall

questions.q: Aavi's aunt likes how her new matka keeps water cool, and to make it look nicer she covers its whole outer surface with a shiny waterproof paint. What will most likely happen to the cooling of the water inside?
questions.a: It will cool much less, since no water can seep out to evaporate
o: It will cool much less, since no water can seep out to evaporate
It will cool more, since the paint keeps all the heat outside
It will cool just the same, since clay is a cold material anyway
It will cool more, since room vapour now condenses on the paint

questions.q: Neha wants to show that the haze in a squeezed plastic bottle (a model of a cloud) appears because of the dust from a burnt piece of newspaper, and not because of the squeezing alone. Which pair of bottles should she compare?
questions.a: Same water, squeezed the same way; burnt paper in one bottle only
o: Same water, squeezed the same way; burnt paper in one bottle only
Burnt paper in both bottles; only one of them is squeezed
Burnt paper and warm water in one; no paper and cold water in the other
Burnt paper in one bottle, squeezed for 3 minutes and then for 6

questions.q: Two pots are filled with water at 32 degrees C. After 4 hours in the same room, the water in a steel pot is at 31 degrees C and the water in an earthen pot is at 24 degrees C. Ramesh says, 'The earthen pot is colder only because clay is a cold material; the water seeping out of it is just wasted.' Check his claim using the data.
questions.a: No. The earthen pot's water fell by 32 - 24 = 8 degrees C against 1 degree C for the steel pot, a difference of 7 degrees C. This happens because water seeps through the surface of the earthen pot and evaporates, and evaporation has a cooling effect. The seeping water is not wasted: it is what cools the water inside.
s: Verdict: No, with the 8 degrees C against 1 degree C (difference 7 degrees C) worked out
Cause: water seeps through the clay surface and evaporates
The seepage is what produces the cooling, so it is not wasted

questions.q:
A vegetable seller in a village with no electricity tests a pot-in-pot cooler. Tomatoes stay fresh for 6 days inside it but only 2 days in an open basket. She tries the cooler in two places. At the shady back of her stall, 1.5 L of water a day keeps the sand moist all day. At the sunny front, where customers can see it, the sand dries out by 2 p.m. unless she adds 3 L a day. All water is carried from a well 300 m away.
(a) Why does the cooler keep tomatoes fresh only while the sand stays moist?
(b) How many litres must she carry over 6 days for the cooler at the back, and how many for the cooler at the front?
(c) Where should she keep the cooler? Use the data and the way the cooler works.
questions.a: (a) The cooling comes from the water in the moist sand evaporating, and evaporation has a cooling effect on the inner pot. Once the sand is dry there is no water left to evaporate, so the cooling stops and the tomatoes warm up. (b) Back: 1.5 x 6 = 9 L. Front: 3 x 6 = 18 L, twice as much. (c) At the shady back. There 9 L over 6 days keeps the sand moist and evaporating all day. At the front she would have to carry 18 L, and on any day she adds too little the sand dries out by 2 p.m. and the cooling stops.
s: (a) evaporation from the moist sand causes the cooling; dry sand, no cooling
(b) 9 L at the back and 18 L at the front
(c) the back: half the water and the sand stays moist, so evaporation keeps cooling

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An earthen pot keeps drinking water cool in summer.
Reason (R): Water vapour is lighter than air, so air containing it rises.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: On a summer afternoon, a park has natural grass on one side and green plastic grass on the other. Natural grass and the soil under it stay moist; plastic grass holds no water. The space around the natural grass feels cooler. Which idea best explains this?
questions.a: Water from the moist grass and soil evaporates, which has a cooling effect
o: Water from the moist grass and soil evaporates, which has a cooling effect
Moist soil under the grass condenses vapour from the air, which cools it
Plastic grass condenses water vapour from the air, which warms the space
Water in the soil freezes at night and keeps the grass cold all day

questions.q:
A village pond holds 2000 kilolitres (kL) of water at the start of summer. For 40 hot days it loses about 15 kL a day by evaporation, and no rain falls. In the monsoon, rain adds 900 kL. The panchayat wants the pond to hold at least 2000 kL again before the next summer.
(a) How much water is left in the pond after the 40 days?
(b) Where did the lost water go, and through which change high in the atmosphere can it come back as rain?
(c) Will the monsoon rain alone bring the pond back to 2000 kL? Show your working, and say what this shows about the water the pond lost.
questions.a: (a) 15 x 40 = 600 kL is lost, so 2000 - 600 = 1400 kL is left. (b) It went into the atmosphere as water vapour by evaporation. High up the air is cool, the vapour condenses into droplets that form clouds, and the droplets join into heavy drops that fall as rain. (c) Yes: 1400 + 900 = 2300 kL, which is 300 kL more than 2000 kL. Water lost by evaporation is not lost from the Earth; it returns as rain in the water cycle (though the rain that falls need not be the very same water).
s: (a) 1400 kL left after losing 600 kL
(b) evaporated as vapour; condensation into clouds, then rain
(c) 2300 kL, 300 kL above the target; water returns in the water cycle

questions.q: An open water tank on a roof in Nagpur loses about 12 L of water a day by evaporation in May; it does not leak. Over the 30 days of a month, ___ L of water goes into the air as water vapour, to come back later as rain.

The seat of Ravi's scooter, parked in the sun, has become too hot to sit on.
(a) Suggest a way to cool it quickly using a little water.
(b) Explain why your method works.
questions.a: (a) Wipe the seat with a wet cloth, or sprinkle a little water on it (and let the air move over it). (b) The water evaporates from the seat, and evaporation has a cooling effect, so the seat cools down.
s: Part (a): put a thin layer of water on the seat (wet cloth or sprinkle)
Part (b): the water evaporates, and evaporation causes cooling

questions.q: In summer, a caretaker sprinkles the same amount of water on the hot terrace of a school at 2 p.m. on two afternoons of the same temperature. On the dry, windy afternoon the terrace feels much cooler afterwards; on the humid, still afternoon it hardly cools at all. Which explanation fits?
questions.a: Water evaporates faster in dry, moving air, and evaporation causes cooling
o: Water evaporates faster in dry, moving air, and evaporation causes cooling
The wind itself is cold, so it cools the terrace whether it is wet or dry
In humid air the water evaporates faster, so it leaves the terrace too soon
In still air the water seeps into the terrace and warms it from below

questions.q:
Read the statements about clouds and rain.
Statement 1: In clouds, water droplets are generally formed around dust particles.
Statement 2: Air containing water vapour rises because water vapour is lighter than air.
Statement 3: Clouds are made of water vapour, which is why we can see them in the sky.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
On a humid morning, a hiker climbing a tall hill walks into a cloud halfway up, though the air at the foot of the hill was clear.
(a) Why does the cloud form high up and not at the foot of the hill?
(b) What is the cloud made of? Correct a friend who says 'water vapour'.
questions.a: (a) As air moves higher above the Earth's surface it becomes cooler and cooler; at a certain height it is cool enough for the water vapour in it to turn into droplets, generally around dust particles. (b) The cloud is made of tiny droplets of liquid water floating in the air, not water vapour; water vapour is invisible, but the cloud can be seen.
s: Part (a): air cools as it rises, until the vapour condenses into droplets
Part (b): tiny liquid droplets, not invisible vapour

questions.q:
Riya's notes on how rain forms are below.
1. The sun boils sea water, and only boiling makes water turn into vapour.
2. Water vapour is heavier than air, so the wind has to lift it.
3. As the air goes higher above the Earth, it becomes warmer.
4. High up, the vapour turns into droplets, generally around dust particles, and these droplets form clouds.
5. Each cloud droplet falls as rain as soon as it forms.
Say whether each line is correct or wrong, and correct every wrong line.
questions.a: 1. Wrong: water evaporates continuously, even at room temperature; it does not need to boil. 2. Wrong: water vapour is lighter than air, so air containing it rises on its own. 3. Wrong: air becomes cooler and cooler as it moves higher. 4. Correct. 5. Wrong: the small droplets float in the air; many join to form bigger drops, and only drops that become heavy enough fall as rain (or, under special conditions, hail or snow).
s: Line 1 corrected: evaporation needs no boiling
Line 2 corrected: vapour is lighter than air and rises
Line 3 corrected: air cools as it rises
Line 4 judged correct
Line 5 corrected: droplets join into heavy drops before falling

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an example of the cooling effect of evaporation?
questions.a: Ice cubes making a glass of nimbu pani cold
o: Ice cubes making a glass of nimbu pani cold
Hand sanitiser feeling cool as it is rubbed in
Water sprinkled on a hot roof cooling it down
A sweaty child feeling cool under a fan

questions.q: True or False? Only water that evaporates from the oceans can come back as rain; water that evaporates from a farmer's wet field is lost from the water cycle. Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Water evaporates into the atmosphere as vapour from the Earth's surface too, not just from the oceans; a wet field, a lake or a puddle all add vapour to the air. That vapour rises, cools, condenses into cloud droplets and returns as rain, hail or snow, so it is part of the same water cycle.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: water evaporating from the land surface also rises, condenses into clouds and returns as rain in the water cycle

questions.q:
A vegetable seller builds a pot-in-pot cooler: a small earthen pot inside a larger one, with wet sand between them, and a wet jute sack over the top.
(a) Why must water be added to the sand regularly?
(b) What is the use of keeping the jute sack wet?
(c) What would happen if the sand were allowed to dry out completely?
questions.a: (a) The water in the sand keeps evaporating; it must be replaced so that evaporation, and therefore cooling, continues. (b) Water from the wet sack also evaporates and cools the top of the inner pot. (c) With no water left to evaporate, the cooling effect would stop and the inside would warm up, so the vegetables would not stay fresh as long.
s: (a) water must be replaced so evaporation and cooling continue
(b) the wet sack also cools by evaporation
(c) dry sand means no evaporation, so no cooling

questions.q: Water from the Bay of Bengal falls as rain on a hill in Meghalaya. Its journey begins: the sea water evaporates, and the air carrying the vapour rises and cools. It ends: heavy drops fall as rain. Which must happen in between?
questions.a: Vapour turns into droplets around dust, and many droplets join into bigger drops
o: Vapour turns into droplets around dust, and many droplets join into bigger drops
The air warms up high above, so the vapour turns into floating droplets
Droplets evaporate back into vapour, so that they can float as clouds
Each tiny droplet falls the moment it forms, joining others on the way

questions.q: Lata says, 'Hail falling on Shimla, rain falling on Chennai and a puddle drying in the sun in my school playground are all part of the same water cycle.' Check her claim.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Water from the oceans and the Earth's surface, including the puddle in her playground, evaporates into the atmosphere as water vapour. The vapour condenses into droplets that form clouds, and the water returns as rain or, under special conditions, as hail. All three belong to this one circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere.
s: Verdict: Yes, the claim is correct
The drying puddle is evaporation from the Earth's surface, which sends water into the atmosphere

questions.q: A ceiling fan runs over a dry steel chair and over a child who is sweating after a game. The chair does not get any cooler, but the child feels cool. Explain the difference.
questions.a: The fan does not cool things by itself. The child has sweat on the skin; the moving air helps the sweat evaporate, and evaporation cools the body. The dry chair has no water to evaporate, so there is no cooling effect.
s: The child's sweat evaporates faster in the moving air
Evaporation cools; the dry chair has no water, so it is not cooled

questions.q:
A school in Jaipur wants to keep its students cooler in summer without buying any new machines.
(a) Judge each idea, saying whether it would help and why: (i) sprinkling water on the classroom roof in the afternoon; (ii) storing drinking water in earthen pots or surahis instead of steel drums; (iii) closing every door and window of a classroom of sweating students so that the air inside is completely still.
(b) Name the one scientific idea behind all your judgements, and use it to suggest one more cooling step the school could take.
questions.a: (a) (i) Helps: the water evaporates from the roof, and evaporation has a cooling effect. (ii) Helps: water seeps through the earthen surface and evaporates, which keeps the drinking water cool. (iii) Does not help: still air slows the evaporation of sweat, so the students lose the cooling they would get with moving air. (b) Evaporation causes cooling. For example, hang a wet jute curtain or sprinkle water on the courtyard floor so that the water evaporates and cools the air around it (or keep the windows open so moving air helps sweat evaporate).
s: (a)(i) roof sprinkling helps by evaporation
(a)(ii) earthen pots help through seepage and evaporation
(a)(iii) still air does not help, as sweat evaporates more slowly
(b) evaporation causes cooling
(b) a fitting extra step that uses evaporation
